newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks remain wobbly, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks remain wobbly, analysts say.

text.p: Malaysia's key stock market index, now trading at 22-month lows, is expected to slide further in coming weeks due to weak technical support, analysts said on Wednesday.
Wobbly technical charts are combining with cloudy fundamental news to pressure the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Composite Index lower in coming weeks, they said.
A Reuters poll of 10 brokerages and fund managers showed that the blue-chip Composite Index could dip to an average 907.2 points, with firmer support at 858.3.
The new resistance level for the index was seen at an average 1,000.8. Forecasts for the immediate support ranged from low 800s to 950 points.

"If charts can speak, we are pretty sure they will unanimously say 'stop rationalising the extent of this fall or being hopeful for supports to hold'," said Vickers Ballas technical analyst Jasmine Yim.
The Composite Index fell to a 22-month low on Tuesday to 945.08 points, the lowest since November 28, 1995.
At the midday break on Wednesday, the index was off 1.34 points to 943.74.
"Once the currency factor comes in I revise myself. 920 is the first hit, 850 is the next," said Nik Ezar Nik Bolia, chief executive officer at RHB Unit Trust Management.
Malaysian stock prices have been in the doldrums since late March, when the central Bank Negara announced curbs on banks' lending to the property sector and for share purchases.
Speculative attacks on regional currencies pushed the ringgit to three-year lows and the market fell in its wake.

Wong Yee Hui, senior research manager at Merrill Lynch, said on a longer term basis, 880 points should provide a strong floor. "All these years, it has held up well. If we break that, it looks like the financial market is telling us we are going into recession," Wong said.

Concerns about possible new capital controls, worries over the trade deficit this year and contagion effect from the Thai baht will continue to sour investor appetite for Malaysian shares, the analysts said.
High domestic interest rates and slowing corporate earnings are also affecting sentiment on the market's fundamentals.
"The bad news are not all factored in yet, they are still coming in," said Pong Teng Swee, assistant research manager at brokerage Seagroatt & Campbell.
The blue-chip index has lost some 22 percent since March 28 and over 25 percent since its peak of 1,278.94 on February 26.
The central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, on Sunday announced that it was limiting non-trade related swap transactions by domestic banks to $2.0 million per overseas customer.
The move was to curb speculative selling of the ringgit and to cool interest rates, but it raised the spectre that Malaysia may announce more capital control measures.

June's huge 2.8 billion ringgit ($1.06 billion) trade deficit and a forecast by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry on Tuesday that Malaysia would register a deficit of 1.65 billion ringgit this year had also pressured sentiment.
Analysts said market valuations were cheap, but they would only cautiously suggest investors to move in.
John Engle, managing director at ABN Amro Hoare Govett said the market's price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is 14 times, below the 15 to 25 times P/E range of the last 10 years.
"Maybe in the next few months we'll be dancing in the streets because the market does so well, but not right now," Engle said.
($1 = 2.64 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
